clue.text: Sounds like covered pleasance where rock merchants gather

indicators.note: the clue says the phrase is heard rather than read, so its spoken form gives the letters

parts.note: a pleasance is a pleasure garden, and one that is covered has a hat on it: hat-on garden

explanation.surface: A riddle about a sheltered pleasure garden where gem dealers congregate.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rock' is slang for a diamond. Hatton Garden is the London street at the centre of the British diamond and jewellery trade.
explanation.definitionFit: This London street is the historic hub of the diamond trade, so dealers in gems meet there.

clue.text: Lady's costume, do some say? It would fit Esau better

indicators.note: what some people say signals that the phrase is spoken, giving a word that sounds the same

parts.note: a lady's costume is her suit

explanation.surface: A question about women's clothing that would suit the biblical Esau better.
explanation.walkthrough: In Genesis Esau was 'a hairy man', unlike his smooth brother Jacob, so a word for shaggy suits him.
explanation.definitionFit: Esau is described in the Bible as hairy, so a word meaning shaggy fits him.

clue.text: Order to weed

explanation.surface: An instruction to go and do some weeding.
explanation.definitionFit: The Most Ancient and Most Noble Order of the Thistle is a Scottish order of chivalry, and the prickly plant is a common weed.

clue.text: Small class rule broken — go charily

indicators.note: something broken is in pieces, so the letters of the following words are reassembled

explanation.surface: A rule for a small class, broken by going about it cautiously.
explanation.definitionFit: Government by a small privileged group is the literal sense of this Greek-derived word.

clue.text: Thick, not clear

explanation.surface: Something described as dense and murky.
explanation.definitionFit: Coarse or dense things are called this, and a sum before deductions is this rather than net or clear.

clue.text: Coarse cloth could be neater round bottom of coat

indicators.note: the reworked letters are placed around the single letter
the word neater could be rearranged into another arrangement of its letters
the bottom of a word written downwards is its last letter

explanation.surface: Rough fabric would look tidier sewn round the hem of a coat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'could be' turns NEATER into RATEEN, and 'round' puts it about T, the last letter of 'coat'.
explanation.definitionFit: Ratteen is an old thick twilled woollen fabric, a kind of coarse material.

clue.text: Exclusion from the Oval?

explanation.surface: A question about someone being barred from the London cricket ground.
explanation.walkthrough: The Oval is a London cricket ground, which makes exclusion from it look like a ban. Ellipse is an old form of ellipsis, the leaving out of words.
explanation.definitionFit: An omission of words is an ellipsis, once spelt this way, and the geometric oval shape bears this name.

clue.text: What Faustus sought to be by Helen's kiss

definitions.text: What Faustus sought to be by Helen's kiss

parts.words: What Faustus sought to be by Helen's kiss
parts.note: in Marlowe's Doctor Faustus he asks Helen of Troy to make him live for ever with a kiss

explanation.surface: A literary question about Marlowe's Faustus and Helen of Troy.
explanation.walkthrough: Marlowe's line is 'Sweet Helen, make me immortal with a kiss.'
explanation.definitionFit: Faustus wanted to be made deathless, given everlasting life, by Helen's kiss.

clue.text: Birdman the first person in the drink

parts.note: Martin is both a bird and a man's name
the first person singular pronoun is I

explanation.surface: A birdman, the first of his kind, ends up in the sea.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The drink' suggests the sea, where a failed birdman lands; here it is just a cocktail.
explanation.definitionFit: A gin and vermouth cocktail is a well-known example of a drink.

clue.text: Kind of bunting seen on tables

definitions.text: Kind of bunting seen on tables

parts.words: Kind of bunting seen on tables
parts.note: bunting suggests festive flags laid on tables, but it is a small bird once served as a delicacy

explanation.surface: Flags decorating party tables.
explanation.walkthrough: Bunting is both decorative flags and a family of finches; this one was a famous dish, eaten whole.
explanation.definitionFit: This small European bird of the bunting family was a prized dish at grand dinners.

clue.text: Mrs Gamp may be on the line to Jingle, that's what the children say

parts.note: Sarah Gamp in Dickens's Martin Chuzzlewit is a nurse, an example of one
RY is an abbreviation for railway, a line
a jingle is a rhyme

explanation.surface: Dickens's Mrs Gamp phoning Mr Jingle, another Dickens character, in a scene the children recite.
explanation.walkthrough: Jingle is also a Dickens character (Pickwick Papers), which makes the line look like a telephone call.
explanation.definitionFit: Children recite traditional verses such as Humpty Dumpty, the classic childhood poems.

clue.text: Prickly pear concealed in the new Utopia

annotationWithheld.why: Prickly pear concealed in the new Utopia: OPUNTIA is UTOPIA rearranged with N, and the only reading uses 'new' both as N and as the anagram signal, one word doing two jobs
annotationWithheld.clue: Prickly pear concealed in the new Utopia

clue.text: Track supporter's ear-piercing device

explanation.surface: Something that holds up a track and pierces ears.
explanation.definitionFit: A railway tie under the rails bears this name, as does a small ring worn to keep a newly pierced ear open.

clue.text: The people here could take us for the old hero

indicators.note: to take something away removes it, so the following word is removed

parts.note: Theseus is the hero of Greek legend who killed the Minotaur
taken as written

explanation.surface: Locals who might mistake us for an ancient hero.
explanation.walkthrough: 'take us for' reads as mistaking us for someone; instead 'take' removes US from THESEUS.
explanation.definitionFit: The demonstrative pronoun points to people near the speaker, those present.

clue.text: Patrons are right among the elect characters

indicators.note: one piece is set among the letters of the other
the characters, or letters, of the word elect are taken and rearranged

parts.note: a lien is a legal right to hold property until a debt is paid

explanation.surface: Customers are said to be right, among the chosen people.
explanation.walkthrough: 'characters' turns ELECT into CTELE, and 'among' sets LIEN between its C and TELE.
explanation.definitionFit: A business's regular customers collectively form its patronage.

clue.text: This is facial make-up, from all accounts

definitions.text: This is facial make-up, from all accounts

parts.words: This is facial make-up, from all accounts
parts.note: make-up suggests cosmetics, but it is a face assembled from witnesses' descriptions

explanation.surface: A remark about cosmetics, as people report.
explanation.walkthrough: The police build a picture of a suspect's face from witnesses' accounts.
explanation.definitionFit: Police composite pictures of suspects are put together from features described by witnesses.

clue.text: "Design for Living' a biography title

parts.note: a biography is a life of someone
a style is a formal title, as in 'styled Duke'

explanation.surface: Noël Coward's play Design for Living cited as the name of a biography.
explanation.walkthrough: Design for Living is a Noël Coward comedy; here it simply means a way of living.
explanation.definitionFit: A person's chosen manner of living is a plan or design for it.

clue.text: He is welcome in the city, though he has no bonds

definitions.text: He is welcome in the city

explanation.surface: A man honoured by his city who is free of ties.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone given the honorary freedom of a city is welcomed there, and a man not enslaved has no chains.

clue.text: Diabolical acts in a variety show

indicators.note: a variety show presents its items in a mixed order, so these letters are mixed

explanation.surface: Terrible turns performed in a music-hall show.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Diabolical' looks like a verdict on the acts, but it is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Of the devil, so fiendish or wicked.

clue.text: Holding high church views with a point

explanation.surface: A churchman with firm Anglo-Catholic opinions who makes a sharp point.
explanation.walkthrough: Spiky (or spikey) is British slang for High Church, Anglo-Catholic leanings in the Church of England.
explanation.definitionFit: Colloquially, a High Churchman is called this, and something with a sharp tip is pointed.

clue.text: Undisciplined characters resent the Right getting tougher

indicators.note: letters out of order, undisciplined, so the word resent is rearranged

parts.note: R is the abbreviation for right

explanation.surface: Unruly people resent the political right becoming harsher.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Undisciplined characters' turns RESENT into STERNE.
explanation.definitionFit: Stricter or more severe in manner is harsher.

clue.text: Unbeliever in Beethoven's opera loses maiden

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: the opera's name loses some of its letters

parts.note: Fidelio is Beethoven's only opera
Io was the maiden of Greek myth loved by Zeus and turned into a heifer

explanation.surface: A heretic in Beethoven's opera loses a young woman.
explanation.walkthrough: Cricket solvers expect maiden to give M; here it is the mythical Io, removed from FIDELIO to leave FIDEL.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone without religious faith, especially from another creed's viewpoint, is a heathen.

clue.text: He mistrusts the old philosopher

explanation.surface: A doubting man compared with a thinker of antiquity.
explanation.definitionFit: A doubter mistrusts claims, and Pyrrho's school of ancient Greek thinkers bore this name.

clue.text: Bloomers revealed in comic acting

indicators.note: the letters are revealed inside the words that follow

explanation.surface: Knickers on show in a comedy routine.
explanation.walkthrough: Bloomers suggests underwear or blunders; here it means plants that flower.
explanation.definitionFit: These spiny succulents produce flowers, so they are things that bloom.

clue.text: Glorious night

explanation.surface: A splendid evening.
explanation.walkthrough: The Glorious Twelfth is 12 August, when the British grouse-shooting season opens; Twelfth Night is Shakespeare's comedy and the eve of Epiphany.
explanation.definitionFit: The ordinal follows 'the Glorious' for the opening of grouse shooting, and precedes 'Night' for Epiphany's eve.

clue.text: Saint who preached — to the fifth form?

definitions.text: Saint who preached — to the fifth form?

parts.words: Saint who preached — to the fifth form?
parts.note: the founder of the Order of Preachers, with a schoolroom hint at dominie, a Scottish word for a schoolmaster who teaches a form

explanation.surface: A saint addressing a class of schoolchildren.
explanation.walkthrough: The Dominican friars are formally the Order of Preachers; the school form suggests a dominie, a schoolmaster.
explanation.definitionFit: The Spanish saint founded the Order of Preachers, the friars named after him.

clue.text: Hunchback's valuation of a horse

parts.note: Shakespeare's hunchbacked Richard III cries that he would give his realm for a horse

explanation.surface: What a hunchback thinks a horse is worth.
explanation.walkthrough: Richard III at Bosworth: 'A horse! A horse! My kingdom for a horse!'
explanation.definitionFit: Richard offered his whole realm in exchange for a horse, so that is the price he set.

clue.text: A French scenario most of the country find apocryphal

parts.note: un is French for a
a scenario is the script of a film

indicators.note: most of a word is all but one of its letters

parts.note: the country, as opposed to the town, is rural

explanation.surface: A French screenplay that most of the nation regards as doubtful.
explanation.walkthrough: 'most of' drops one R from RURAL, leaving URAL.
explanation.definitionFit: Apocryphal texts are those not accepted into the biblical canon, so not part of holy writ.
